input.project: Calculate garden water savings and write an accessible article about the result.

project.request: Calculate the garden savings while independently planning an article; then combine the two completed results into the final article.

Write an accessible article of 100 to 160 words using BOTH selected completed artifacts: the math specialist result supplies the weekly litres saved, and the editorial outline supplies the exact headline and themes. Include the exact numeric math result in decimal digits and the unit litres per week, the outline headline, community cooperation and a practical takeaway. End with your saved byline. Return the article directly.

# The Quiet Garden 99e11499

Every Saturday morning, neighbors at the community garden pull a single hose across nineteen raised beds. Each bed holds 32 plants, and each plant needs about 15 litres of water in a week. Multiply it out, and the garden's own records show a weekly saving of 9120 litres — water that once ran down drains and evaporated without helping a single tomato.

The saving was not the work of one clever gardener. It came from cooperation: a shared rota that assigns watering days, a watering log that keeps track of what was done, and neighbors who mention to one another when a bed already looks damp. Small habits, repeated by many hands, produced a total no single person would have reached.

Read the figure carefully. It is an estimate drawn from garden records, not a promise about future bills, and it assumes each plant received that amount of water.

One takeaway to carry home: check the soil before you turn on the hose, then write down what you did. The garden already proves the method works.

By Wren Editor (writer-76b5104d)

# The Quiet Garden 99e11499

Every Saturday morning, neighbors at the community garden pull a single hose across nineteen raised beds. Each bed holds 32 plants, and each plant needs about 15 litres of water in a week. Multiply it out, and the garden's own records show a weekly saving of 9120 litres — water that once ran down drains and evaporated without helping a single tomato.

The saving was not the work of one clever gardener. It came from cooperation: a shared rota that assigns watering days, a watering log that keeps track of what was done, and neighbors who mention to one another when a bed already looks damp. Small habits, repeated by many hands, produced a total no single person would have reached.

Read the figure carefully. It is an estimate drawn from garden records, not a promise about future bills, and it assumes each plant received that amount of water.

One takeaway to carry home: check the soil before you turn on the hose, then write down what you did. The garden already proves the method works.
